title: I Fixed a Tractor Using John Deere's Self-Repair Service. Farmers Aren't Sold on It
gist: A year after launching its Pro Service self-repair software amid right-to-repair lawsuits and a $99 million settlement, John Deere has only about 1,000 daily users out of roughly 1.8 million US farms, and named plaintiffs and repair advocates say the program still withholds the deepest diagnostic access needed for complex, multi-fault repairs.

themes.theme: Adoption is negligible despite the product working for simple fixes

insights.claim: A year after John Deere introduced its Pro Service self-repair software in 2025, the service has only about 1,000 daily users, a tiny fraction given there are roughly 1.8 million farms in the US, and Deere itself frames its challenge as awareness rather than product quality.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Extremely low adoption (~1,000 daily users vs. 1.8M farms) despite regulatory and legal pressure to offer self-repair suggests either weak product-market fit, distribution failure, or farmer distrust — a red flag for any thesis that self-repair programs will meaningfully offset dealership service revenue for Deere.
insights.quote: A year on, John Deere says its service has about a thousand daily users—a relatively small number, given that there are somewhere around 1.8 million farms in the US.

insights.claim: Farmer and named plaintiff Jared Wilson, who farms 3,000 acres in Missouri, does not use Pro Service and says he doesn't know anyone who does; he says farmers he knows instead use cracked versions of repair software obtained on gray markets rather than pay John Deere.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth (citing Jared Wilson)
insights.so_what: Evidence of an active gray/pirate market for tractor diagnostic software is a direct signal of unmet demand at Deere's price point and a leakage channel that undercuts the Pro Service subscription business model.
insights.quote: Wilson does not use Pro Service. He doesn't know anyone who does, saying the farmers he knows tend to use cracked versions of the software they find on gray markets instead of giving their money to John Deere.
insights.locator: Data as a Service section, Wilson quotes

insights.claim: Pro Service works well for simple, single-fault repairs (the author fixed a disconnected water-in-fuel sensor in a couple of minutes using guided software instructions) but users report it breaks down when multiple simultaneous diagnostic codes are present, since the software doesn't guide troubleshooting priority across compounding faults.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth (citing Jared Wilson)
insights.so_what: The product's core limitation — poor handling of compound/multi-fault diagnostics — is exactly the scenario where professional repair services capture the most revenue, meaning Deere's self-repair tool may be structurally designed (or limited) to leave the highest-value repairs with dealers.
insights.quote: If you have multiple failures, you have to figure out where to start... If you have three different or four different diagnostic codes, where do you start in the tree to figure out what's wrong?
insights.locator: Data as a Service section, Wilson quote on multiple failures

insights.claim: John Deere's Pro Service pricing starts at $195 per year for an individual machine, scaling to $4,995 per year for access to every machine in a fleet, and $5,995 per year for agricultural and turf services access — a tiered subscription model layered on top of hardware ownership.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Concrete recurring-revenue pricing tiers ($195/machine up to $5,995/year fleet access) show Deere is building a SaaS-like diagnostics layer on top of equipment sales — relevant to modeling Deere's services revenue growth and margin mix.
insights.quote: Prices start at an annual cost of $195 per individual machine. For bigger operations or independent repair shops, the price to access every machine in John Deere's fleet starts at $4,995 a year.

insights.claim: John Deere's newer machines can have upward of 50 electronic controllers, and the company has added an AI chatbot called JD to its Operations Center self-repair tool specifically to help owners navigate this rising complexity.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth (citing Jahmy Hindman)
insights.so_what: Rising per-machine controller counts (up to 50) mean equipment complexity is outpacing simple repair manuals, driving Deere toward AI-assisted diagnostics — a template other heavy-equipment OEMs may follow as their machines add electronics.
insights.quote: As the tractor products grow in size, they also grow in number of controllers that are necessary in order to make it all work... So it can be super complex.

insights.claim: In April 2026 John Deere agreed to pay a $99 million settlement to equipment owners over burdensome repair costs, and in July 2026 it separately settled an FTC lawsuit requiring it to make its products more repairable; the company admitted no wrongdoing in either case and both settlements were not yet final at time of writing.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Two concurrent legal actions (class action + FTC) totaling meaningful settlement costs represent an ongoing legal/regulatory liability overhang and reputational risk for Deere, and set a precedent other right-to-repair-targeted OEMs may face.
insights.quote: In April, the company agreed to pay out a $99 million settlement to its equipment owners to pay back burdensome repair costs. In July, the company settled a separate lawsuit brought by the US Federal Trade Commission that would require the company to make its products more repairable.

insights.claim: Named plaintiff Jared Wilson has publicly called the $99 million settlement ruling 'fundamentally flawed' and remains skeptical that Deere's current self-repair concessions represent genuine change rather than a minimal legal compliance response.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth (citing Jared Wilson)
insights.so_what: A named plaintiff's public skepticism that Deere's Pro Service is a genuine reform (rather than minimal legal compliance) signals continued litigation and advocacy risk even after settlements, meaning the right-to-repair overhang on Deere is not fully resolved.
insights.quote: It's taken a class action lawsuit and FTC action to get them to come this far... If you believe what they're saying now—that this is actually it and we're getting everything we've asked for—then I've got some oceanfront property in Arizona to sell you.
insights.locator: Data as a Service section, Wilson quote

insights.claim: Repair.org board member Willie Cade argues John Deere behaves as a monopolist whose real customer is Wall Street rather than the farmer, framing the self-repair dispute as a shareholder-value-versus-customer-access conflict.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth (citing Willie Cade)
insights.so_what: Frames the right-to-repair fight explicitly as a conflict between Deere's shareholder-value incentives (parts/service margin) and farmer access, a lens relevant to assessing regulatory and reputational risk to Deere's services revenue model.
insights.quote: They're just monopolists that want to make money and as much as they possibly can... Their real customer is not the farmer. Their real customer is Wall Street.
insights.locator: Data as a Service section, Cade quote

themes.theme: Structural limits on farmer diagnostic access

insights.claim: John Deere uses 'Product Improvement Plans' (PIPs) to notify owners of known equipment issues, but a PIP is only issued after Deere's system has gathered enough information and internally verified a problem, meaning farmers facing a novel issue have no official troubleshooting path until Deere catches up — leaving a persistent information gap between when a farmer discovers a problem and when Deere documents it.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: The PIP process structurally lags real-world failures, meaning even farmers using official channels can face extended downtime on novel issues — a downtime/cost risk not solved by subscribing to Pro Service.
insights.quote: If a user faces a novel problem with how a machine works, it would still take time for that issue to get back to John Deere, which would verify it, then issue a PIP in Pro Service.

insights.claim: Farmers, including plaintiff Jared Wilson, say John Deere still withholds the deepest level of diagnostic access needed to resolve the most difficult and complex equipment problems, even under the current self-repair offering.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth (citing Jared Wilson)
insights.so_what: Persistent gatekeeping of top-tier diagnostic access even post-settlement suggests Deere's competitive moat around complex repairs (and associated dealer service revenue) remains largely intact despite regulatory pressure.
insights.quote: They're still not giving us access to that next level that we have to have for some of the most difficult problems that we encounter.
insights.locator: Paragraph after PIPs discussion, Wilson quote
